kurals.tamil:
நயந்தவர்க்கு நல்காமை நேர்ந்தேன் பசந்தவென்
பண்பியார்க்கு உரைக்கோ பிற.
kurals.transliteration:
nayandhavarkku nalkaamai naerndhaen pasandhaven
panpiyaarkku uraikko pira
kurals.meaning: I myself agreed to let my loving husband go away; now that my body has turned pale with longing, to whom else can I complain about it?
kurals.elementary: Imagine you told your best friend, ‘It’s okay, go on the trip without me,’ and then you missed them so much you felt sick. You can’t really complain to anyone, because you said yes! The wife in this couplet feels exactly that way.
kurals.university: Chapter 119 of the karpiyal (married love) section turns on pasalai or pasappu (பசலை / பசப்பு), the sallow, pallid tint that classical Tamil poetics treats as the visible sign of a wife’s grief in separation; both ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net title the chapter பசப்புறு பருவரல் (pasappuṟu paruvaral, ‘the distress of having become pallid’), while this edition’s chapter list spells it பசப்பறு. In this opening couplet the heroine admits that she nērntēn (நேர்ந்தேன், ‘consented’) to nalkāmai (நல்காமை, literally ‘not showing grace’, which the modern commentators Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all gloss as the husband’s separation); having agreed, she has forfeited the right to complain, hence yārkku uraikkō piṟa, ‘to whom else shall I tell it?’. In the traditional commentary associated with Parimelazhagar the chapter is voiced by the heroine to her confidante (tōḻi), and the irony of complaining while saying one cannot complain is the point. Pope renders: ‘I willed my lover absent should remain; / Of pining’s sickly hue to whom shall I complain?’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: After Dushyanta leaves the hermitage to return to his capital, Shakuntala, who has accepted his going, sits so lost in thoughts of him that she fails even to notice the sage Durvasas at the door, and her friends must keep her sorrow to themselves.
hinduism.explanation: Kalidasa shows a young wife who agreed to her husband’s departure and is then consumed by an absence she cannot openly lament.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Shakuntala has consented to the parting and is left with a private grief she has no one to tell.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known scene, not checked against a translation this session; consent to parting and silent grief match, though Shakuntala’s pallor is not the focus.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if ye find my beloved, that ye tell him, that I am sick of love.”
christianity.explanation: The bride, separated from her beloved, has no way to reach him and must ask others to carry word of her love-sickness.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine asks the same question in reverse: she is sick with love and has no one she can rightly tell.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; love-sickness in separation and the problem of whom to tell match well, though the bride has not consented to the parting.

islam.quote_or_event: “I only complain of my suffering and my grief to Allāh, and I know from Allāh that which you do not know.”
islam.explanation: Jacob, grieving for the absent Joseph and rebuked by his sons for his endless sorrow, says he will bring his complaint to God alone.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also has no human listener for her grief; Jacob’s answer is that the only fitting hearer is God.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; the ‘to whom shall I complain’ motif matches, though Jacob grieves for a son, not a husband.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The heart knoweth its own bitterness; And with its joy no stranger can intermeddle.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs observes that the deepest sorrows of the heart are its own and cannot really be shared with another.
judaism.tie_back: The heroine’s pallor is exactly such a bitterness known only to her own heart, with no one to whom she can hand it over.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a general proverb on unsharable grief, not about lovers or consent to parting.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “So don’t make anything dear, for it’s dreadful to be far from what’s dear.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that holding someone dear makes distance from them a source of dread and pain.
buddhism.tie_back: The heroine has discovered just this: being far from the one she loves has turned her body pale with grief.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; the pain of distance from the beloved matches, though the Buddhist remedy is non-attachment rather than reunion.

jainism.quote_or_event: “When the daughter of the king heard of the ordination of the Gina, laughter and gaiety forsook her, and she was overwhelmed with affliction.”
jainism.explanation: Rajimati, betrothed to Arishtanemi, learns that he has turned away from the wedding to become a monk, and her joy vanishes.
jainism.tie_back: As in the Kural, a woman is left to bear the sorrow of a beloved’s departure, though Rajimati soon turns it into her own renunciation.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; the grief of a forsaken bride fits, but Rajimati did not consent to the parting and her story leads to renunciation, not reunion.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Penelope recalls that when Odysseus set out for Troy he took her by the wrist, entrusted the household to her care and told her what to do if he did not return; she accepted, and for twenty years she weeps for him in private while the suitors crowd her hall.
greek_mythology.explanation: Penelope agreed to her husband’s going and is left to grieve with no one in the house she can trust with her sorrow.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s wife, Penelope consented to the parting and now pines with no proper listener.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not checked against a translation this session; consent and lonely grief match, though Homer does not dwell on pallor.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle observes that people in grief are comforted when friends share their sorrow, as if the burden were lightened by being divided.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, the presence of a sympathetic friend is one of the main reliefs of sorrow.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine lacks exactly that relief: she has no one to share her grief with, because she agreed to its cause.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not checked word for word this session; it states the general principle her situation denies her.

kurals.tamil:
அவர்தந்தார் என்னும் தகையால் இவர்தந்தென்
மேனிமேல் ஊரும் பசப்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
avardhandhaar ennum thakaiyaal ivardhandhaen
maenimael oorum pasappu
kurals.meaning: Proud that it was given to me by him, this pallor climbs all over my body and spreads as if it owned it.
kurals.elementary: Think of a sticker your favourite person gave you: you might put it everywhere, proud of it because of who gave it. The wife says the pale colour on her skin acts like that sticker. It spreads all over her, proud because her husband ‘gave’ it to her by going away.
kurals.university: The heroine personifies pasappu (பசப்பு) as a proud guest: avar tantār ennum takaiyāl, ‘with the dignity of “he gave it”’, it ivarntu (இவர்ந்து, ‘mounting, climbing’) and ūrum (ஊரும், ‘creeps, spreads, rides’) over her mēni (மேனி, body, complexion). Takai here is ‘worth, pride’; Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar both render the pallor as spreading ‘with pride’ (பெருமிதம்) because the lover caused it. Pope’s rendering takes ūrum in the sense of riding: ‘“He gave”: this sickly hue thus proudly speaks, / Then climbs, and all my frame its chariot makes.’ The conceit, that even the affliction is precious because it comes from him, is characteristic of the karpiyal chapters and of the traditional reading associated with Parimelazhagar, in which the wife cannot fully resent what her husband’s absence has given her. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Meghaduta the exiled yaksha pictures his wife at home, wasted and pale with separation, lying on one side of her bed like the last thin crescent of the moon, her beauty itself changed by her grief for him.
hinduism.explanation: Kalidasa makes the wife’s altered, pallid body the very sign and record of her husband’s absence.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine says the same: the pallor spreading over her is his gift, the mark his absence has left on her.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not checked against a translation this session; the wasted, pale wife is a close image, though the Kural adds the twist of pride.

christianity.quote_or_event: “From henceforth let no man trouble me: for I bear in my body the marks of the Lord Jesus.”
christianity.explanation: Paul treats the scars he has suffered for Christ as marks of belonging that he carries with pride.
christianity.tie_back: The heroine’s pallor is likewise a bodily mark she wears proudly because it comes from the one she loves.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; the proud bodily mark of a beloved matches structurally, but Paul’s marks are of apostolic suffering, not love-sickness.

islam.quote_or_event: “And he turned away from them and said, ‘Oh, my sorrow over Joseph,’ and his eyes became white from grief, for he was [of that] a suppressor.”
islam.explanation: Jacob’s long grief for his absent son visibly changes his body, whitening his eyes.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, separation from a beloved writes itself on the body as a change of colour.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; a strong parallel of grief changing bodily colour, though the bond is parent and child, not husband and wife.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Set me as a seal upon thy heart, As a seal upon thine arm; For love is strong as death, Jealousy is cruel as the grave; The flashes thereof are flashes of fire, A very flame of the LORD.”
judaism.explanation: The beloved asks to be pressed onto the lover’s heart and arm like a seal, a mark that shows whose they are.
judaism.tie_back: The heroine’s pallor is that kind of seal: a mark on her body that proclaims whose love caused it.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; the love-as-bodily-seal image is a partial match, since the Song’s seal is chosen while the Kural’s pallor is suffered.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From what’s dear is born grief, from what’s dear is born fear. For one freed from what’s dear there’s no grief — so how fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha traces grief back to its source in holding someone dear.
buddhism.tie_back: The heroine says her pallor was ‘given by him’; the Dhammapada agrees that the grief is born from the dear one, though it draws the opposite lesson.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; both trace grief to the beloved, but the Buddha counsels release while the heroine treasures the gift.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Pleasant things (by themselves) do not cause indifference nor emotions (as anger, &c.); but by either hating or loving them, a man undergoes such a change through delusion.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana teaches that inner and outer changes come not from objects or other people but from one’s own attachment to them.
jainism.tie_back: The heroine credits her lover with ‘giving’ her pallor; the Jain view would locate the cause in her own attachment, an honest contrast to the Kural’s conceit.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; offered as a contrast, since Jain teaching would reject the Kural’s idea that the beloved is the giver of the change.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sappho describes what happens to her when she sees the beloved: her tongue breaks, a thin fire runs under her skin, her eyes see nothing, sweat pours down, trembling seizes her, and she becomes greener than grass, seeming to herself little short of dying.
greek_mythology.explanation: In this famous poem love shows itself as a physical change of colour, a pallor or greenness that takes over the whole body.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s pasappu that ‘climbs over my body’ is the same idea: love’s pallor spreading across the lover’s frame.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known lyric, not checked against a translation this session; Greek lyric poetry rather than myth, and Sappho’s pallor comes from the beloved’s presence, not absence.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Lucretius warns that lovers waste their strength and are worn out with toil, their bodies and fortunes spent while they live at another’s beck and call.
philosophy.explanation: The Epicurean poet treats love’s physical toll on the lover as a reason for caution.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s pallor is that physical toll, but where Lucretius sees only harm, the heroine sees a gift from her husband.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not checked word for word this session; it matches love’s bodily cost but not the heroine’s pride in it.

kurals.tamil:
சாயலும் நாணும் அவர்கொண்டார் கைம்மாறா
நோயும் பசலையும் தந்து.
kurals.transliteration:
saayalum naanum avarkondaar kaimmaaraa
noayum pasalaiyum thandhu
kurals.meaning: He took away my beauty and my modesty, and in exchange he gave me love-sickness and this pallor.
kurals.elementary: Imagine trading your shiny new toy for a broken one and a bad cold. Not a fair swap! The wife jokes sadly that her husband made a swap like that: he took her bright looks and her shyness, and left her with sadness and a pale face.
kurals.university: The couplet is built on the language of exchange: kaimmāṟā (கைம்மாறா, ‘as a return, in exchange’) the husband took (koṇṭār) her sāyal (சாயல், grace, soft beauty) and nāṇ (நாண், modesty, the sense of shame proper to a woman in Sangam poetics) and gave (tantu) nōy (நோய், the disease of love) and pasalai (பசலை). The loss of nāṇ ties back to chapter 114 (நாணுத் துறவுரைத்தல், ‘declaring the abandonment of modesty’). Solomon Pappaiah reads the exchange as happening at the very moment of parting; Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar keep the bare trade. Pope renders: ‘Of comeliness and shame he me bereft, / While pain and sickly hue, in recompense, he left.’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Gita Govinda Radha’s companion tells Krishna how Radha, pining for him, has wasted away: her ornaments feel like burdens, her beauty fades and she languishes in the bower thinking only of him.
hinduism.explanation: Jayadeva describes separation stripping the beloved of her loveliness and leaving only longing.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine names the same exchange: her beauty taken, love-sickness left in its place.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the general content of these cantos, not checked against a translation this session; viraha (separation) imagery matches, though the canto references are approximate.

christianity.quote_or_event: “To appoint unto them that mourn in Zion, to give unto them beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness …”
christianity.explanation: The prophet promises a divine exchange in which mourners receive beauty in place of ashes.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine describes the exact reverse trade: her beauty taken, sorrow and pallor given back.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; an inverse parallel built on the same idea of exchanged beauty and grief, not a direct match.

islam.quote_or_event: In Nizami’s Layla and Majnun, Layla, kept apart from Majnun, slowly loses her bloom; the poet describes her as fading and wasting in secret, hiding her grief from those around her until it consumes her.
islam.explanation: Separation in the great Persian romance takes the beloved’s beauty and leaves only hidden suffering.
islam.tie_back: As in the Kural, love’s parting has traded away beauty for illness and pallor.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the romance’s general narrative, not checked against a translation this session; a Persian literary work from Muslim culture rather than scripture.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Call me not Naomi, call me Marah; for the Almighty hath dealt very bitterly with me. I went out full, and the LORD hath brought me back home empty.”
judaism.explanation: Naomi (‘pleasant’) says her very name no longer fits: her life has exchanged sweetness for bitterness.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also describes an exchange that has left her changed: grace and modesty gone, pallor and sorrow in their place.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; the full-to-empty exchange matches in shape, but Naomi grieves bereavement, not a lover’s absence.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The former courtesan Ambapali, now a nun, describes how her once-celebrated beauty has changed with time: her black hair has turned like hemp bark, her eyes and skin have lost their lustre, and she concludes that the words of the Truth-speaker hold true.
buddhism.explanation: Ambapali’s verses watch beauty being taken away and replaced by its opposite.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also inventories lost beauty, though she blames her husband’s absence, while Ambapali sees the impermanence of all forms.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of well-known verses, not checked against a translation this session; the loss of beauty matches, but Ambapali’s cause is age, not separation.

jainism.quote_or_event: The emperor Sanatkumara, famous for his beauty, invited two gods who had praised it to see him in full splendour at court; they told him that in that short time his body had already been taken over by disease, and on seeing it was so he renounced the world.
jainism.explanation: Jain narrative uses Sanatkumara to show how quickly beauty can be taken and illness given in its place.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine experiences the same swift exchange, her beauty for sickness, though she blames her husband’s absence rather than impermanence.
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-attested Jain story, not checked against Johnson’s translation this session; a next-best match about lost beauty, not love-sickness.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The nymph Echo, spurned by Narcissus, hides in the woods; her love clings to her and grows with grief, sleepless care wastes her body, her skin shrinks and the bloom of her body vanishes into the air until only her voice and bones remain.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid shows unrequited, separated love literally consuming a lover’s beauty and body.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Echo’s fate dramatises the Kural’s complaint: love has taken her beauty and left only sickness and wasting.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not checked against a translation this session; beauty wasted by love matches, though Echo’s love was never returned.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Diotima’s account, Eros, the child of Poverty and Resource, is not delicate and beautiful as people think but always poor, hard and squalid, barefoot and homeless, sharing his mother’s neediness.
philosophy.explanation: Plato’s Symposium portrays love itself as a state of lack rather than of beauty.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine finds the same: love has left her poorer, stripped of beauty and modesty.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not checked word for word this session; love-as-lack is a loose fit to a concrete exchange of beauty for pallor.

kurals.tamil:
உள்ளுவன் மன்யான் உரைப்பது அவர்திறமால்
கள்ளம் பிறவோ பசப்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
ulluvan manyaan uraippadhu avardhiramaal
kallam piravo pasappu
kurals.meaning: I think only of him, and all I speak of is his goodness; yet the pallor has come all the same. Is it not a trick?
kurals.elementary: Imagine you did all your homework and studied hard, and still got a bad mark. You’d say, ‘That’s not fair, I did everything right!’ The wife says the same: she thinks about her husband all day and only says good things about him, yet the sad pale colour still came. It feels like a trick.
kurals.university: The heroine protests that she has kept faith in thought and speech: uḷḷuvan maṉ yāṉ (உள்ளுவன் மன் யான், ‘I do indeed think of him’), uraippatu avar tiṟam (உரைப்பது அவர் திறம், ‘what I speak is his worth’), so the pallor must be kaḷḷam (கள்ளம், ‘deceit, theft’) or come by some other way (piṟavō). The implied logic, made explicit by the commentators, is that constant remembrance should keep the absent one ‘present’, so the pallor of separation has no right to appear. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah render kaḷḷam as vañcaṉai/vañcakam (treachery); Kalaignar instead asks how the pallor came ‘without my knowing or by some other path’. Pope: ‘I meditate his words, his worth is theme of all I say, / This sickly hue is false that would my trust betray.’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Uddhava brings Krishna’s message to Vraja, the gopis can speak of nothing but Krishna’s deeds and qualities, remembering every pastime with him, and yet their constant remembrance only deepens the grief of his absence.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata’s gopis show a love that lives on unceasing remembrance and praise of the absent beloved.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also thinks and speaks only of her husband’s virtues, and is still overtaken by the pallor of separation.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known chapter, not checked against a translation this session; remembrance and praise without relief is a close fit.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I remembered God, and was troubled: I complained, and my spirit was overwhelmed. Selah.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist finds that remembering the one he longs for brings not comfort but trouble.
christianity.tie_back: The heroine likewise remembers her beloved constantly and is surprised that remembrance does not keep sorrow away.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; remembrance followed by distress matches, though the psalmist’s longing is for God, not a spouse.

islam.quote_or_event: “They said, ‘By Allāh, you will not cease remembering Joseph until you become fatally ill or become of those who perish.’”
islam.explanation: Jacob’s sons warn him that his unceasing remembrance of the absent Joseph is wasting his body.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also never stops remembering her beloved, and that very remembrance has not spared her body from wasting pallor.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; unceasing remembrance consuming the body is a close parallel, though the love is a father’s.

judaism.quote_or_event: “His mouth is most sweet; Yea, he is altogether lovely. This is my beloved, and this is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem.”
judaism.explanation: Separated from him and asked what makes him special, the bride answers with a long praise of her beloved’s every quality.
judaism.tie_back: Like the bride, the Kural’s heroine says that all she speaks of is her absent husband’s excellence.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; praising the absent beloved matches well, though the Song does not raise the puzzle of why pallor still comes.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Whatever a monk keeps pursuing with his thinking & pondering, that becomes the inclination of his awareness.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha observes that whatever the mind dwells on repeatedly shapes the whole bent of a person.
buddhism.tie_back: The heroine dwells on her husband all day, and the Buddhist view would say that this very dwelling bends her toward the grief she complains of.
buddhism.source: Dvedhavitakka Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 19 (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; it explains rather than shares her puzzle, and its context is monastic training of thought.

jainism.quote_or_event: Among the forms of arta-dhyana (sorrowful, afflicted meditation) the Tattvartha Sutra lists the mind’s repeated dwelling on how to regain something agreeable from which one has been separated.
jainism.explanation: Jain psychology names constant longing for a lost beloved object as a kind of painful concentration that binds karma.
jainism.tie_back: The heroine’s ceaseless thinking about her absent husband is exactly this ‘afflicted meditation’, and the Jain view would see her pallor as its fruit rather than a trick.
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from general knowledge of the sutra, not checked against Tatia’s translation this session; sutra numbering differs slightly between recensions.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: While her husband Ceyx is away at sea, Alcyone counts the nights, prays daily to Juno for his safe return and thinks of nothing but him, unaware that he has already drowned.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ovid’s Alcyone keeps faith through constant thought and prayer for an absent husband.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like Alcyone, the Kural’s heroine thinks only of her absent husband, and still sorrow finds its way to her.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode, not checked against a translation this session; the faithful, preoccupied wife matches, but Alcyone’s tragedy is a death, not a temporary absence.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza defines longing (desiderium) as the desire to possess something that is kept alive by remembering it, while the remembrance of other things excludes its existence.
philosophy.explanation: For Spinoza, remembering an absent beloved breeds not satisfaction but a sorrowful longing.
philosophy.tie_back: This explains the heroine’s puzzle: her constant remembrance of him is precisely what feeds the longing that turns her pale.
philosophy.source: Spinoza, Ethics III, Definitions of the Affects 32 (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known definition, not checked word for word this session; a close philosophical account of why remembrance brings pallor.

kurals.tamil:
உவக்காண்எம் காதலர் செல்வார் இவக்காண்என்
மேனி பசப்பூர் வது.
kurals.transliteration:
uvakkaan-em kaadhalar selvaar ivakkaan-en
maeni pasappoor vadhu
kurals.meaning: Look there, my lover is walking away; and look here, the pallor is already creeping over my body.
kurals.elementary: Picture an ice cream on a hot day: the moment you take it out of the freezer, it starts to melt. The wife says that the moment her husband started walking away, before he was even out of sight, her face started going pale.
kurals.university: The couplet’s force lies in two deictic phrases: uvakkāṇ (உவக்காண், ‘see, over there’, using the mid-distance demonstrative u-) and ivakkāṇ (இவக்காண், ‘see, right here’), setting the departing husband and the arriving pallor side by side as simultaneous events; pasappu ūrvatu (பசப்பு ஊர்வது) is ‘the creeping of pallor’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan keep the present tense (‘there he goes; here it spreads’), whereas Solomon Pappaiah reads it as a memory of how, even in earlier partings, the pallor came the instant he left, so that the present absence must be worse. Pope’s version, ‘My lover there went forth to roam; / This pallor of my frame usurps his place at home’, adds the idea of the pallor taking his place. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Akrura takes Krishna away to Mathura, the gopis of Vraja stand watching his chariot as it goes, gazing after it until the banner and even the dust it raised can no longer be seen, and are left stricken and lamenting.
hinduism.explanation: The Bhagavata dwells on the exact moment of the beloved’s departure and the grief that begins as he recedes from sight.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural catches the same instant: ‘there he goes’ and, at once, ‘here comes the pallor’.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known chapter, not checked against a translation this session; watching the beloved depart and grief beginning at once is a strong fit.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And when he had spoken these things, while they beheld, he was taken up; and a cloud received him out of their sight.”
christianity.explanation: The disciples watch their beloved master depart before their eyes until he is hidden from them.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘look there, he goes’ freezes the same moment of watching the loved one leave.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; the watched departure matches, but the Ascension is a joyful theological event, not a lover’s parting.

islam.quote_or_event: Rumi opens the Masnavi with the reed-flute, which complains of separation and says that ever since it was cut from the reed-bed its lament has made men and women weep.
islam.explanation: For the Sufi poet, the moment of being cut off from the beloved source is where all longing and lament begins.
islam.tie_back: The Kural places the onset of the pallor at that same moment of severance, as the beloved walks away.
islam.source: Rumi, Masnavi I.1-2 (paraphrase of R.A. Nicholson’s translation)
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of famous opening lines, not checked against Nicholson’s text this session; separation as the origin of grief fits, though Rumi’s beloved is ultimately divine.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I opened to my beloved; But my beloved had turned away, and was gone. My soul failed me when he spoke. I sought him, but I could not find him; I called him, but he gave me no answer.”
judaism.explanation: The bride finds her beloved gone and at once her soul fails within her.
judaism.tie_back: In both texts the beloved’s going and the lover’s collapse happen in the same breath.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; the immediate failing at the beloved’s departure matches closely.

buddhism.quote_or_event: On his wedding day the Buddha’s half-brother Nanda follows the Buddha to the monastery carrying his bowl, while his bride Janapada Kalyani calls after him to come back quickly; he is ordained and afterwards pines for her.
buddhism.explanation: The canonical story of Nanda captures a bride watching her groom walk away on the very day of their union.
buddhism.tie_back: The scene is the Kural’s ‘there he goes’ seen from the bride’s doorway, though the Buddhist story follows the monk rather than her grief.
buddhism.source: Nanda Sutta, Udana 3.2, and Dhammapada commentary on verses 13-14 (paraphrase)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-attested story, not checked against a translation this session; the bride’s call after the departing groom is a strong image, but the text says nothing of her pallor.

jainism.quote_or_event: Riding in his wedding procession to marry Rajimati, Arishtanemi hears the cries of animals penned for the wedding feast, gives his ornaments to his charioteer and turns away to renounce the world, leaving the bride whose wedding was about to begin.
jainism.explanation: In the Jain account the groom turns back at the very threshold of marriage out of compassion for living beings.
jainism.tie_back: Rajimati’s sorrow begins the moment her bridegroom turns away, the same instant the Kural captures.
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase checked against Jacobi’s text on sacred-texts.com; the departure scene fits, but Jainism presents it as a model of renunciation, not a cause for lament.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid’s Heroides Laodamia writes to Protesilaus that as his ship sailed out of Aulis she watched it while she could, and when it vanished she fell senseless and turned pale, lifeless as the dead.
greek_mythology.explanation: Laodamia describes her body failing and paling at the very moment her husband’s ship disappeared.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Her letter is almost the Kural verbatim in narrative form: there goes the husband, here comes the pallor.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known epistle, not checked against a translation this session; a very close parallel of wife, departure and instant pallor.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Plato describes the lover’s soul as warmed and growing its wings while the beloved is present, but when they are parted the passages dry up and close, and the soul is stung all over and in anguish until it sees the beloved again.
philosophy.explanation: In the Phaedrus the lover’s pain begins as soon as the beloved is absent, as an almost physical change.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural records the same immediacy: absence begins and the bodily change, the pallor, begins with it.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not checked word for word this session; immediate pain of absence matches, though Plato’s lover is in a philosophical, not married, relationship.

kurals.tamil:
விளக்கற்றம் பார்க்கும் இருளேபோல் கொண்கன்
முயக்கற்றம் பார்க்கும் பசப்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
vilakkatram paarkkum irulepoal kon-kan
muyakkatram paarkkum pasappu
kurals.meaning: Just as darkness waits for the lamp to fail, the pallor waits for the moment my husband’s embrace loosens.
kurals.elementary: When you blow out a candle, the dark rushes in right away, as if it had been waiting just outside the light. The wife says the sad pale colour is like that dark: it waits, and as soon as her husband’s hug ends, it rushes in.
kurals.university: A celebrated simile: viḷakku aṟṟam pārkkum iruḷ (விளக்கு அற்றம் பார்க்கும் இருள், ‘darkness that watches for the lamp’s lapse’) is set against koṇkaṉ muyakku aṟṟam pārkkum pasappu (‘pallor that watches for the lapse of my husband’s embrace’). Aṟṟam (அற்றம்) means a gap, failing or unguarded moment; pārkkum is ‘watches for, lies in wait’. Koṇkaṉ (கொண்கன்) is a classical word for husband, traditionally associated with the seashore (neytal) landscape. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses the embrace’s aṟṟam as its slackening, Solomon Pappaiah as its loosening, and Kalaignar as the moment the tight hold relaxes. Pope: ‘As darkness waits till lamp expires, to fill the place, / This pallor waits till I enjoy no more my lord’s embrace.’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; the transliteration kon-kan follows ytamizh.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Hanuman first finds Sita in Ravana’s Ashoka grove, Valmiki likens the grieving, pale, emaciated wife separated from Rama to a flame veiled in smoke and to the moon’s crescent dimmed by clouds.
hinduism.explanation: The Ramayana pictures the separated wife as a light obscured, her radiance darkened by the absence of her husband.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural uses the same light-and-darkness image: without the husband’s presence the wife’s brightness is overtaken by pallor.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of well-known similes, not checked against a translation this session; sarga numbers are approximate and differ between editions.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then Jesus said unto them, Yet a little while is the light with you. Walk while ye have the light, lest darkness come upon you: for he that walketh in darkness knoweth not whither he goeth.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus warns that darkness is waiting to come in as soon as the light he brings is withdrawn.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s darkness ‘waiting for the lamp to fail’ is the same picture applied to a wife’s pallor in the beloved’s absence.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; the waiting-darkness image matches closely, but the context is spiritual light, not married love.

islam.quote_or_event: “And from the evil of darkness when it settles”
islam.explanation: The short sura of refuge treats the settling darkness of night as a power from which one seeks protection.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s darkness and pallor are similarly forces poised to settle over the unprotected moment.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; only the image of encroaching darkness matches, the verse has nothing to do with lovers.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Until the day breathe, and the shadows flee away, Turn, my beloved, and be thou like a gazelle or a young hart Upon the mountains of spices.”
judaism.explanation: The Song pairs the beloved’s presence with light and the fleeing of shadows.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural uses the reverse of this image: when the beloved’s embrace lapses, the shadow of pallor returns.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; it shares the light-shadow-beloved imagery but not the simile of darkness lying in wait.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “When this world is ever ablaze, why this laughter, why this jubilation? Shrouded in darkness, will you not see the light?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha pictures ordinary life as shrouded in darkness and urges people to seek the light.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s darkness waiting to cover the lamp is a similar image, though for the Buddha the darkness is ignorance rather than a lover’s grief.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a shared lamp-and-darkness image only, the theme differs.

jainism.quote_or_event: “He who is passionately fond of ‘colours,’ will come to untimely ruin; just as an impassioned moth which is attracted by the light rushes into death.”
jainism.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana uses the moth and the lamp to show how attachment to what the senses love leads to suffering.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural also turns on a lamp image; the Jain lesson would be that dependence on the beloved’s ‘light’ is what lets the darkness of pallor in.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; it shares a lamp image and the theme of suffering from attachment, but the simile works differently.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Every night Hero set a lamp in her tower so that Leander could swim the Hellespont to her; on a stormy night the wind blew the lamp out, darkness took the strait, and Leander drowned.
greek_mythology.explanation: In the legend the lovers’ union depends on the lamp, and when it fails the darkness brings the lovers’ ruin.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural makes the same link between a failing lamp and the onset of a lover’s grief.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known legend, not checked against a translation this session; the lamp-darkness-lovers link is striking, though the outcome is death, not pallor.

philosophy.quote_or_event: La Rochefoucauld observes that absence lessens small passions and increases great ones, just as the wind puts out candles but fans a fire.
philosophy.explanation: The moralist uses the image of a flame exposed to the wind to describe what absence does to love.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural pairs love and a failing lamp in the same way; the heroine’s love is the great kind that absence inflames into pallor.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous maxim, not checked against a translation this session; the flame-and-absence image is close, though the logic differs.

kurals.tamil:
புல்லிக் கிடந்தேன் புடைபெயர்ந்தேன் அவ்வளவில்
அள்ளிக்கொள் வற்றே பசப்பு.
kurals.transliteration:
pullik kidandhen pudaipeyarndhaen avvalavil
allikkol vatre pasappu
kurals.meaning: I lay held close in his arms; I merely turned aside a little, and in that instant the pallor swept over me as if scooping me up.
kurals.elementary: You know how a snowman starts melting the second the sun comes out? The wife says she was cuddled up safe and happy, turned over for just a moment, and in that tiny moment the sad pale colour grabbed her, like a big scoop.
kurals.university: The couplet heightens the previous one by shrinking the interval to almost nothing: pullik kiṭantēṉ (புல்லிக் கிடந்தேன், ‘I lay embracing’), puṭai peyarntēṉ (புடைபெயர்ந்தேன், ‘I shifted to one side’), avvaḷavil (‘in just that much’), the pallor aḷḷik koḷvaṟṟē (அள்ளிக்கொள்வற்றே, ‘was like something scooped up in handfuls’, i.e. it came in a rush). Solomon Pappaiah frames it as a recollection of an earlier occasion, making the point a fortiori for the present long absence, while Kalaignar and Puliyur Kesikan keep it as a vivid present. Pope: ‘I lay in his embrace, I turned unwittingly; / Forthwith this hue, as you might grasp it, came on me.’ The treatment is tasteful and hyperbolic, the conventional rhetoric of the heroine’s extreme sensitivity. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Mahabharata’s story of Nala and Damayanti, Nala, ruined and wandering in the forest with his wife, leaves her while she sleeps; Damayanti wakes to find him gone and searches the forest crying out for him, wasting with grief.
hinduism.explanation: The Nalopakhyana gives the classic Indian scene of a wife who was beside her husband one moment and abandoned the next.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Damayanti passes from closeness to desolation in the space of a single turning in sleep.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode, not checked against a translation this session; the sudden loss of a husband’s presence matches, though Nala truly deserts her.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But the days will come, when the bridegroom shall be taken away from them, and then shall they fast in those days.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus says the joy of the bridegroom’s presence gives way to fasting and mourning as soon as he is taken away.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural shows the same switch in miniature: closeness, a moment’s parting, and grief at once.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; the bridegroom-taken-away motif fits, but it is a figure for Jesus and his disciples.

islam.quote_or_event: “They are a clothing for you and you are a clothing for them.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes husband and wife as each other’s garment, giving closeness, covering and protection.
islam.tie_back: In the Kural, the instant that ‘garment’ of closeness slips away, the wife is left exposed to pallor.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API (excerpt); it describes spousal closeness, not the grief of its loss.

judaism.quote_or_event: “By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth; I sought him, but I found him not.”
judaism.explanation: The bride reaches for her beloved in the night and finds he is not there.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also turns in the night and finds the closeness gone, with grief rushing in.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a close match of a night-time reaching for the beloved who is not there.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Don’t ever — regardless — be conjoined with what’s dear or undear. It’s painful not to see what’s dear or to see what’s not.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that being bound to a dear one makes even a moment of not seeing them painful.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine shows how sharp that pain can be: a moment of not holding her husband is enough.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; the pain of not seeing the dear one matches, though the Buddhist lesson is non-attachment.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Pleasures bring only a moment’s happiness, but suffering for a very long time, intense suffering, but slight happiness; they are an obstacle to the liberation from existence, and are a very mine of evils.”
jainism.explanation: The sons of Bhrigu tell their father that the happiness of pleasure is brief while the suffering it brings is long.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural shows that imbalance in a single night: a moment’s closeness, and at the slightest parting a flood of pallor.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; it explains why the joy is fragile but, as a call to renunciation, does not share the Kural’s tender view of married love.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Psyche, forbidden to look on her unseen husband, raises a lamp over him as he sleeps; a drop of hot oil wakes Cupid, who at once flies away, leaving her alone and grieving.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Apuleius’s tale a single small movement in the bridal chamber ends the lovers’ closeness in an instant.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also turns for a moment and finds closeness gone and grief already upon her.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known tale, not checked against a translation this session; a Latin novel retelling a Greek myth; the instant loss matches, but Psyche’s act is a broken prohibition.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Aristophanes’ speech, humans are halves of an original whole who, once divided, long for each other, throw their arms around each other, and pine away when apart, wishing never to be separated even for a moment.
philosophy.explanation: Plato’s Aristophanes explains love as the desire of two halves to be whole, so that any separation is felt as a wound.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine feels exactly that: the slightest parting from her other half brings immediate suffering.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known speech, not checked word for word this session; a strong match for love that cannot bear even momentary separation.

kurals.tamil:
பசந்தாள் இவள்என்பது அல்லால் இவளைத்
துறந்தார் அவர்என்பார் இல்.
kurals.transliteration:
pasandhaal ival-enpadhu allaal ivalaith
thurandhaar avar-enpaar il
kurals.meaning: People only say, ‘She has turned pale’; no one says, ‘He has left her.’
kurals.elementary: Imagine your friend broke your toy, and everyone said, ‘Why is that toy broken? You must be careless!’ but nobody said, ‘Your friend broke it.’ That feels unfair. The wife feels the same: everybody notices her pale face, but nobody says it’s because her husband went away.
kurals.university: A couplet about public opinion (alar, the village gossip that runs through the Kamattuppal): people say pasantāḷ ivaḷ (பசந்தாள் இவள், ‘she has grown pale’), but none says tuṟantār avar (துறந்தார் அவர், ‘he has abandoned her’). Tuṟa- is the same root as tuṟavu, ‘renunciation, forsaking’, giving the complaint a sharp edge. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read the first clause as blame (பழி) directed at the woman for showing her grief, while the man’s departure, the real cause, escapes comment. Pope: ‘On me, because I pine, they cast a slur; / But no one says, “He first deserted her.”’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Shakuntala arrives at Dushyanta’s court, the king, under Durvasas’s curse, does not remember her; it is she whose honesty and conduct are questioned before the assembly, while the husband who forgot her is not blamed.
hinduism.explanation: Kalidasa stages a scene in which public suspicion falls on the wife rather than on the husband who failed her.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine complains of the same imbalance: people remark on her, not on the man who left.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known scene, not checked against a translation this session; the misdirected blame fits, though Shakuntala’s case involves a curse, not pallor.

christianity.quote_or_event: The scribes and Pharisees bring to Jesus a woman taken in adultery and set her in the midst for judgment; the man is not brought, and Jesus answers that whoever is without sin should cast the first stone.
christianity.explanation: The episode exposes a public judgment that singles out the woman while the man escapes notice.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s complaint has the same shape: the woman’s condition is talked about, the man’s part is ignored.
christianity._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage; the one-sided blame matches structurally, but the context is a charge of adultery, quite unlike a faithful wife’s pallor.

islam.quote_or_event: “Why, when you heard it, did not the believing men and believing women think good of themselves [i.e., one another] and say, ‘This is an obvious falsehood’?”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an rebukes the community for repeating talk that wrongly blamed a woman instead of assuming the best.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also suffers from talk that blames her while ignoring the true cause.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API; a rebuke of unjust gossip about a woman, though its occasion was a slander, not a husband’s absence.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Look not upon me, that I am swarthy, That the sun hath tanned me; My mother’s sons were incensed against me, They made me keeper of the vineyards; But mine own vineyard have I not kept.”
judaism.explanation: The bride asks onlookers not to stare at her darkened skin, explaining that it was caused by others who sent her out under the sun.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, she knows people will judge her changed colour without seeing who caused it.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a strong match for a woman’s changed complexion being judged without regard to its cause, though the cause is not a lover.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “O Atula! Indeed, this is an ancient practice, not one only of today: they blame those who remain silent, they blame those who speak much, they blame those who speak in moderation. There is none in the world who is not blamed.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha observes that public blame is universal and arbitrary.
buddhism.tie_back: The heroine discovers the same arbitrariness: the village blames her pallor, never his absence.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; it fits the theme of unfair public blame, though not the specific imbalance between wife and husband.

jainism.quote_or_event: Anjana Sundari, neglected for years by her husband Pavananjaya, is visited by him secretly before he leaves for war; when she is found to be with child, her mother-in-law accuses her of misconduct and drives her out, and even her own family refuses to take her in, while no one questions the absent husband.
jainism.explanation: In this Jain narrative, the mother of Hanuman bears all the blame for a situation her absent husband created.
jainism.tie_back: Her story is the Kural’s complaint writ large: everyone speaks of what has happened to her, and no one speaks of him.
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-attested Jain story (also in Vimalasuri’s Paumacariya), not checked against Johnson’s translation this session; strong on misdirected blame, though the details differ from simple pallor.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Virgil’s Rumour (Fama) spreads through the cities of Libya the tale of Dido’s love for Aeneas and her neglect of her kingdom; when Aeneas sails away, it is Dido who is left disgraced and talked about.
greek_mythology.explanation: In the Aeneid public talk fastens on the abandoned woman while the departing hero sails on.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine complains of the same: the talk is all about her, never about the man who left.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not checked against a translation this session; a Roman epic on Greek-Trojan myth; Dido was not married to Aeneas in the Kural’s sense.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle holds that praise and blame are properly given only for voluntary actions, while what is involuntary, done under compulsion or in ignorance, deserves pardon and sometimes pity.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, blame should follow responsibility.
philosophy.tie_back: By that standard the village has it backward: her pallor is involuntary, while his departure was his choice.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not checked word for word this session; it supplies the principle behind her complaint, not a parallel scene.

kurals.tamil:
பசக்கமன் பட்டாங்கென் மேனி நயப்பித்தார்
நன்னிலையர் ஆவர் எனின்.
kurals.transliteration:
pasakkaman pattaangen maeni nayappiththaar
nannilaiyar aavar enin
kurals.meaning: If he who sweetly persuaded me to let him go is himself well and in good standing, then let my body turn as pale as it will.
kurals.elementary: Imagine your big brother goes away to camp and you miss him so much you feel sad. But then you think, ‘As long as he’s having fun and is safe, I don’t mind being a bit sad.’ That is what the wife says: if her husband is doing well, she doesn’t mind the pale colour.
kurals.university: Here the heroine turns from complaint to self-sacrifice: pasakka maṉ (பசக்க மன், ‘let it grow pale indeed’), paṭṭāṅku (பட்டாங்கு, ‘as it actually is, to its full measure’) eṉ mēṉi, if nayappittār (நயப்பித்தார், ‘he who made me consent by sweet persuasion’, from nayam, pleasantness) is nannilaiyar (நன்னிலையர், ‘of good standing’). Commentators divide on nannilaiyar: Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah read it as ‘good, blameless’, so the verse is half ironic, while Kalaignar reads ‘is well, prospers’, making it a wish for his welfare; the Pope translation (‘in good estate remain’) supports the latter, and the alternative rendering on ytamizh, ‘if he is clear of guilt’, supports the former. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Narada Bhakti Sutra, taking the gopis of Vraja as its model, describes the highest love as finding one’s happiness in the beloved’s happiness, and says that a love lacking this is not true love.
hinduism.explanation: The bhakti tradition treats tat-sukha-sukhitvam, being happy in the beloved’s happiness, as the mark of pure love.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine shows exactly this: if he is well, her own suffering does not matter.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from general knowledge of the sutras, not checked against a translation this session; the sutra numbers are approximate and the text is devotional, not marital.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up …”
christianity.explanation: Paul defines love as patient endurance that does not put itself first.
christianity.tie_back: The heroine’s willingness to suffer the pallor so long as her husband prospers is love that ‘suffereth long’.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; patient, self-forgetting love matches the spirit, though the verse is general, not about separation.

islam.quote_or_event: “… but give [them] preference over themselves, even though they are in privation. And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his soul — it is those who will be the successful.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an praises those who put others’ good before their own even when they themselves are in need.
islam.tie_back: The heroine likewise prefers her husband’s well-being to her own, accepting her pallor as the price.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API (excerpt); self-preference for another matches, but the verse concerns the Ansar and the emigrants, not spouses.

judaism.quote_or_event: Jonathan, heir to Saul’s throne, loves David as his own soul; he strengthens David in hiding and tells him that David will be king over Israel and he himself will be second to him, gladly giving up his own claim for his friend’s good.
judaism.explanation: The Bible’s great story of devoted friendship shows a love that wishes the beloved well at one’s own cost.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine shows the same spirit: let her suffer, provided the one she loves fares well.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of well-known passages, not checked against the JPS text this session; self-giving love fits, though it is friendship rather than married love.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Karaniya Metta Sutta teaches wishing that all beings be happy and at ease, and cherishing them with a boundless heart, as a mother would protect her only child with her own life.
buddhism.explanation: Buddhist loving-kindness wishes others’ welfare without condition, even at the cost of oneself.
buddhism.tie_back: The heroine’s wish that her husband fare well, whatever it costs her own body, is a personal form of that goodwill.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a very well-known sutta, not checked against a translation this session; metta is universal and non-attached, unlike the heroine’s particular love.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Shame upon my life, that I have been forsaken by him! it is better I should turn nun.”
jainism.explanation: Rather than resent Arishtanemi for leaving, Rajimati resolves to follow the same path of renunciation he has chosen, and later attains perfection.
jainism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, she does not curse the one who left; she accepts her own loss and honours his choice.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; her acceptance parallels the Kural’s, but Rajimati turns to renunciation rather than wishing a husband well in worldly life.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Admetus is fated to die unless someone takes his place, his wife Alcestis alone agrees to die in his stead so that he may live.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Euripides’ play Alcestis is the model of a wife who accepts her own suffering for her husband’s welfare.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine shows the same spirit on a smaller scale: let her body suffer so long as he fares well.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known play; a strong match for a wife accepting suffering for her husband’s good, though Alcestis’s sacrifice is her life.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle notes that friendship consists more in loving than in being loved, and points to mothers who delight in loving their children and wish them well even when they receive no love in return.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, the deepest affection wishes the other’s good for its own sake, regardless of return.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine’s wish that her husband prosper, whatever it costs her, is love of exactly this kind.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not checked word for word this session; it states the principle but its example is maternal, not marital.

kurals.tamil:
பசப்பெனப் பேர்பெறுதல் நன்றே நயப்பித்தார்
நல்காமை தூற்றார் எனின்.
kurals.transliteration:
pasappenap paerperudhal nandre nayappiththaar
nalkaamai thootraar enin
kurals.meaning: It is fine for me to be known as ‘the pale one’, so long as people do not slander him who persuaded me to let him go for his unkindness.
kurals.elementary: Imagine your friend forgot your birthday, and you felt sad. If people started saying mean things about your friend, you might say, ‘It’s okay, just call me the sad one, but please don’t be mean to my friend.’ That’s what the wife says: call me pale, but don’t blame him.
kurals.university: The chapter closes on the heroine’s protectiveness: pasappu eṉap pēr peṟutal naṉṟē (பசப்பெனப் பேர்பெறுதல் நன்றே, ‘it is good to get the name of pallor’), if people tūṟṟār (தூற்றார், ‘do not slander, broadcast in blame’) the nalkāmai (நல்காமை, ‘lack of grace, unkindness’) of nayappittār (‘him who won my consent’). The verse answers 1188: there she resented that people blamed her and not him; here she would rather keep the blame herself than have his name spoiled, a turn the commentators read as the ideal of the karpu (chaste, loyal) wife. Solomon Pappaiah takes the people as those who would otherwise abuse him for not returning; Kalaignar as those who would call him loveless. Pope: ‘’Tis well, though men deride me for my sickly hue of pain; / If they from calling him unkind, who won my love, refrain.’ Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; the opening verb nalkāmai echoes Kural 1181, framing the chapter.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Lakshmana leaves the pregnant Sita at Valmiki’s hermitage on Rama’s orders because of the people’s talk, Sita sends word that she grieves not for herself but wishes Rama to protect his good name and treat his subjects as he would his own kin.
hinduism.explanation: In the Uttara Kanda Sita, though abandoned, chooses to guard her husband’s reputation rather than accuse him.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine makes the same choice: let her bear the name of pallor, so long as no one blames him.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode, not checked against a translation this session; sarga numbering differs between editions and the Uttara Kanda is considered a later layer.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And above all things have fervent charity among yourselves: for charity shall cover the multitude of sins.”
christianity.explanation: Peter teaches that love covers over the faults of the one loved rather than exposing them.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine covers her husband’s unkindness the same way, keeping the reproach on herself.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; love covering the other’s fault matches the heroine’s choice closely.

islam.quote_or_event: “… and whoever screened a Muslim, Allah will screen him on the Day of Resurrection.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet praises those who cover the faults of others rather than exposing them.
islam.tie_back: The heroine would screen her husband’s unkindness from public blame, accepting the talk about her own pallor instead.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sunnah.com (excerpt); the virtue of concealing another’s faults matches, though the hadith speaks of fellow believers generally.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Hatred stirreth up strifes; but love covereth all transgressions.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs contrasts hatred, which exposes and inflames, with love, which covers another’s wrongs.
judaism.tie_back: The heroine’s love covers her husband’s unkindness; she will take the name of pallor rather than let him be blamed.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria; a close match for love that covers the beloved’s fault.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Let none find fault with others; let none see the omissions and commissions of others. But let one see one’s own acts, done and undone.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha counsels against dwelling on others’ faults and failures.
buddhism.tie_back: The heroine refuses to dwell on her husband’s neglect and would have no one else dwell on it either.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; not finding fault with another matches, though the Dhammapada turns attention to oneself rather than to protecting a loved one.

jainism.quote_or_event: In the Silappatikaram, Kannagi, whose husband Kovalan has left her for years for the dancer Madhavi, lays aside her ornaments and lives quietly in grief; when he returns ruined, she speaks no reproach and gives him her anklets to rebuild their life.
jainism.explanation: The Tamil epic portrays a wife who bears long neglect without exposing her husband’s fault.
jainism.tie_back: Kannagi lives out the Kural’s choice: she endures the marks of grief herself rather than speak against her husband.
jainism.source: Ilango Adigal, Silappatikaram, Puhar Kandam (cantos 4 and 9) (paraphrase)
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase from general knowledge, not checked against a translation this session; the epic contains Jain elements and its author is traditionally said to be a Jain monk, but that attribution is debated, so this is a Tamil-Jain-adjacent source rather than canonical scripture.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Of the fifty daughters of Danaus ordered to kill their husbands on the wedding night, Hypermnestra alone spared hers, Lynceus, helping him escape and accepting her father’s anger and imprisonment rather than harm him.
greek_mythology.explanation: Hypermnestra chooses to bear punishment herself rather than let harm come to her husband.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine makes a gentler version of the same choice: let the reproach fall on her, not on him.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known myth, not checked against a translation this session; self-sacrifice to protect a husband fits, but the situation is far more extreme.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Works of Love Kierkegaard devotes a deliberation to the theme ‘Love hides a multitude of sins’, arguing that the loving person does not discover or publicise the faults of the beloved but mitigates and hides them.
philosophy.explanation: Kierkegaard treats concealing the beloved’s fault as an act of love, not of deception.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine practises exactly that: she would rather be known as ‘the pale one’ than have his unkindness exposed.
philosophy.source: Søren Kierkegaard, Works of Love (1847), Second Series, V (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the deliberation’s argument, not checked against a translation this session; a close philosophical match, though Kierkegaard writes of Christian love generally.
